answerBody:
Congress should hold S. 5653 and rewrite it more narrowly. The November 9 cloture vote, 73 to 25, only opened debate on a substitute carried by H.R. 2347. It did not make the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act a durable governing framework for data-center grid costs or energy buildout.

The package contains a useful cost rule. As summarized by the Bipartisan Policy Center, a new Federal Power Act section would stop utilities from shifting the incremental generation, transmission, and distribution costs of new data centers and high-density loads of 20 megawatts or more onto other customers, and would require financial assurances before upgrades are built. Grid Strategies estimated roughly $55 billion in data-center transmission charges over ten years, about $35 billion more than under current policy. That allocation problem is real and separable. The House already passed a weaker Ratepayer Protection Act, H.R. 9340, by 417 to 3. Senate cloture failed 57 to 43 on September 30 because Democrats, including Martin Heinrich, wanted a binding standard rather than a state duty merely to consider one. A stronger standalone cost statute is therefore politically available. It does not require rewriting NEPA, the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act, or Section 106.

Those rewrites are the reason to hold. The Congressional Research Service summary of the introduced bill, R49506, dated November 5, describes a 150-day challenge window, restricted standing, appellate venue, and a general bar on vacatur or injunction for NEPA violations unless extra criteria are met. Separate project-certainty language would, with narrow exceptions, stop agencies from altering many permits in effect on or after September 16, 2026. On November 8, the National Congress of American Indians still urged a no vote and withdrawal of the historic-preservation title. NCAI said the manager's amendment left agencies able to end Section 106 review in their sole discretion, treat short consultation clocks as satisfied by a written reply, bypass Tribal Historic Preservation Officers, and leave construction in place during remand. A weekend review of a roughly 494-page substitute is not government-to-government consultation.

The strongest counterargument is Sheldon Whitehouse's claim that this is a valuable bird in the hand. Democrats won both chambers on November 3, but the new Congress does not convene until January 3, 2027, and will not have 60 Senate votes. Waiting could lose transmission siting, deadlines, and the cost floor if President Trump's support, already conditioned on wind approvals, evaporates. That risk is genuine, but not decisive. Enactment would lock a technology-neutral shortcut and permit-durability regime into statutes the next Congress could not readily unwind, while grandfathering approved data-center arrangements. Rhodium Group's estimate of $50 to $78 lower average household bills in 2040 bundles permitting changes with cost shifting and is not a reason to accept the bargain.

Congress should keep the 20-megawatt cost floor, financial assurances, and early-exit recovery, and negotiate transmission timelines with tribes and communities at the table. It should not pass this package, judicial-review limits and Section 106 rewrite included, before the new Congress convenes.
rationale: The posture is to hold the package for a narrower rewrite. The November 9 vote only opened debate, the data-center cost floor is separable from the NEPA, permit-certainty, and Section 106 changes, and NCAI's November 8 objection shows the manager's amendment did not cure the tribal-consultation problem. The counterargument that a post-midterm Congress may not reassemble 60 votes is acknowledged but does not justify locking those constraints in before January 3, 2027. The word-counting capability confirmed answerBody is within range.
